claim: The cervical cancer screening programme continued in Denmark throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, in contrast to most of the world.
source: In contrast to most of the world, the cervical cancer screening programme continued in Denmark throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and introduction sections of the manuscript.

claim: The study included 2,220,000 invited women (in 1,466,353 individuals) aged 23-64 years old invited to participate in cervical cancer screening from 2015 to 2021.
source: Altogether, 2,220,000 invited women (in 1,466,353 individuals) were included in the study.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section and supported by data from the Cervical Cancer Screening Database.

claim: Before the pandemic, 36% of invited women participated in screening within 90 days, 54% participated within 180 days, and 65% participated within 365 days.
source: Before the pandemic, 36% of invited women participated in screening within 90 d, 54% participated within 180 d, and 65% participated within 365 d.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by data analysis.

claim: At the start of the pandemic, participation in cervical cancer screening within 90 days was lower during pre-lockdown (PR = 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56–0.59) and first lockdown (PR = 0.76; 95% CI: 0.75–0.77) compared with previous years.
source: At the start of the pandemic, participation in cervical cancer screening within 90 d was lower (pre-lockdown PR = 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56–0.59 and first lockdown PR = 0.76; 95% CI: 0.75–0.77) compared with the previous years.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with statistical analysis using prevalence ratios.

claim: A reduction in participation within 180 days was seen during pre-lockdown (PR = 0.89; 95% CI: 0.88–0.90) and first lockdown (PR = 0.92; 95% CI: 0.91–0.93).
source: A reduction in participation within 180 d was also seen during pre-lockdown (PR = 0.89; 95% CI: 0.88–0.90) and first lockdown (PR = 0.92; 95% CI: 0.91–0.93).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Allowing for 365 days to participation, only a slight reduction (3%) in participation was seen with slightly lower participation in some groups (immigrants, low education, and low income).
source: Allowing for 365 d to participation, only a slight reduction (3%) in participation was seen with slightly lower participation in some groups (immigrants, low education, and low income).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section of the abstract with supporting data analysis.

claim: Denmark has a population of approximately 5.8 million inhabitants.
source: The study was set in Denmark, which has a population of approximately 5.8 million inhabitants (Statistics Denmark, 2021).
evidence: Cited from Statistics Denmark, 2021.

claim: Denmark has a tax-funded healthcare system with universal access to healthcare for all residents including national screening programmes for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer.
source: Denmark has a tax-funded healthcare system, with universal access to healthcare for all residents including national screening programmes for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section describing the setting.

claim: In Denmark, all women aged 23-64 years old are invited to participate in cervical cancer screening every 3 years (women aged 23-49 years old) or every 5 years (women aged 50-64 years old).
source: In Denmark, all women aged 23–64 y old are invited to participate in cervical cancer screening every 3 y (women aged 23–49 y old) or every 5 y (women aged 50–64 y old; Bonde et al., 2022).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation to Bonde et al., 2022.

claim: In Denmark, three main waves of the COVID-19 pandemic occurred: in the spring of 2020, in the winter of 2020/2021, and again in the winter of 2021/2022.
source: In Denmark, three main waves of the COVID-19 pandemic have occurred that is, in the spring of 2020, in the winter of 2020/2021, and again in the winter of 2021/2022 (Statens Serum Institut, 2021a).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021a.

claim: Population-wide restrictions ('lockdown') were imposed in Denmark on 11 March 2020.
source: In efforts to minimise the spread of the infection, population-wide restrictions ('lockdown') were imposed in Denmark 11 March 2020, and subsequently, large parts of the society were closed down.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section describing the pandemic timeline.

claim: Extensive testing facilities were set up in Denmark from May 2020, providing COVID-19 tests free-of-charge to the whole population.
source: Extensive testing facilities were set up in Denmark from May 2020, providing COVID-19 tests free-of-charge to the whole population (Pottegård et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation to Pottegård et al., 2020.

claim: In Denmark, laymen were trained to perform COVID-19 tests, which is in contrast to many other countries where healthcare personnel were allocated to perform COVID-19 tests.
source: In Denmark, laymen were trained to perform COVID-19 tests, which is in contrast to many other countries where healthcare personnel were allocated to perform COVID-19 tests.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section comparing Denmark's approach to other countries.

claim: Vaccination against COVID-19 began in December 2020 in Denmark, and by March 2022, approximately 81% of the population had received two doses, and more than 61% had received three doses of the vaccine.
source: Vaccination against COVID-19 began in December 2020 in Denmark, and a high vaccination coverage has been achieved, and by March 2022, approximately 81% of the population had received two doses, and more than 61% had received three doses of the vaccine (Statens Serum Institut, 2021b).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021b.

claim: The Danish College of General Practitioners recommended general practitioners to postpone routine cervical smears during a 4 week period in March/April 2020.
source: At the same time, however, at the national televised press conferences, the health authorities asked the Danish population to stay at home if possible, and concurrently, the Danish College of General Practitioners recommended general practitioners to postpone routine cervical smears during a 4 wk period in March/April 2020 (Dansk Selskab for Almen Medicin, 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the Introduction with citation to Dansk Selskab for Almen Medicin, 2020.

claim: Invitations and reminders were sent out throughout the pandemic in Denmark.
source: Nevertheless, the cervical cancer screening programme continued – and invitations and reminders were sent out – throughout the pandemic in Denmark.
evidence: Directly stated in the Introduction describing the screening programme operations.

claim: It is estimated that the disruptions to the cervical cancer screening programmes in high-income countries because of the pandemic could potentially increase cervical cancer cases by up to 5-6% and increase the number of cervical cancers detected at a higher stage.
source: It is estimated that the disruptions to the cervical cancer screening programmes in high-income countries because of the pandemic could potentially increase cervical cancer cases by up to 5–6% and increase the number of cervical cancers detected at a higher stage (Smith et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Smith et al., 2021 in the Introduction.

claim: Marked reductions in the number of women screened for cervical cancer during the early phase of the pandemic have been reported in many other countries.
source: Marked reductions in the number of women screened for cervical cancer during the early phase of the pandemic have been reported in many other countries (Castanon et al., 2022; Cancer Registry of Norway, 2020; Meggetto et al., 2021; Ivanuš et al., 2021), whilst the participation in cervical cancer screening during the pandemic in Denmark has not yet been described.
evidence: Cited from multiple sources (Castanon et al., 2022; Cancer Registry of Norway, 2020; Meggetto et al., 2021; Ivanuš et al., 2021) in the Introduction.

claim: Participation in cervical cancer screening is generally reduced among women of lower socio-economic status.
source: It is well known that participation in cervical cancer screening is generally reduced among women of lower socio-economic status (Harder et al., 2018) and among immigrant women (Hertzum-Larsen et al., 2019; Badre-Esfahani et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Harder et al., 2018 in the Introduction.

claim: Participation in cervical cancer screening is generally reduced among immigrant women.
source: It is well known that participation in cervical cancer screening is generally reduced among women of lower socio-economic status (Harder et al., 2018) and among immigrant women (Hertzum-Larsen et al., 2019; Badre-Esfahani et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Hertzum-Larsen et al., 2019 and Badre-Esfahani et al., 2020 in the Introduction.
